Title: Definition of epidemiology
QuestionText: Which of the following BEST describes epidemiology?
Hint: Think about populations rather than individual patients.
Feedback: Epidemiology studies both the distribution of disease and its determinants.
Choice1: The clinical study of disease in individual patients
Choice2: The study of the distribution and determinants of disease in populations
Choice3: The laboratory study of pathogens that cause infectious disease
Choice4: The branch of statistics used to analyze medical data
Fb1: Incorrect. That is clinical medicine, which treats individuals.
Fb2: Correct. Distribution, determinants, and application to control health problems.
Fb3: Incorrect. That is microbiology, not epidemiology.
Fb4: Incorrect. Statistics is a tool epidemiology uses, not the field itself.

Title: Fundamental assumptions
QuestionText: Select ALL of the fundamental assumptions of epidemiology.
Feedback: Disease does not occur at random, and determinants can be identified systematically.
Choice1: Human disease does not occur at random
Choice2: Every disease has a single sufficient cause
Choice3: Disease determinants can be identified by systematic investigation
Choice4: Disease frequency is uniform across all populations
Fb1: Correct. This is the first fundamental assumption.
Fb2: Incorrect. Most diseases have multiple contributing causes.
Fb3: Correct. This is the second fundamental assumption.
Fb4: Incorrect. Variation across groups is what makes epidemiologic study possible.

Title: Person-time accrual
QuestionText: Person-time stops accruing when a person develops the disease of interest, dies, or is lost to follow-up.
Hint: Can a person be at risk of a disease they already have?
Feedback: Person-time accrues only while someone is at risk and under observation.
Fb1: Correct. Observation time ends at the outcome, death, or loss to follow-up.
Fb2: Incorrect. Once the outcome occurs the person is no longer at risk.

Title: Selection bias in a cohort
QuestionText: Describe one way selection bias could arise in a prospective cohort study, and how you would reduce it.
Hint: Consider who is lost between enrollment and the end of follow-up.
Feedback: Differential loss to follow-up is the classic answer here.
InitialText: Source of bias: ... How I would reduce it: ...
AnswerKey: A strong answer names differential loss to follow-up related to both exposure and outcome, and proposes active retention or a sensitivity analysis.

Title: Measure using person-time
QuestionText: Which measure of disease frequency uses person-time in its denominator?
Hint: It is a rate, not a proportion.
Feedback: Incidence rate uses accumulated person-time at risk in the denominator.

Title: Measures and denominators
QuestionText: Match each measure of disease frequency to its denominator.
Hint: Only one of these uses time in the denominator.
Feedback: Rates use person-time; risks and prevalences use counts of people.
Match3: Total population at a point in time

Title: Outbreak investigation steps
QuestionText: Put the first four steps of an outbreak investigation in order.
Hint: You cannot describe cases before you define what counts as one.
Choice1: Confirm the existence of an outbreak
Choice4: Describe cases by person, place, and time
Fb1: This comes first. Verify the diagnosis and that counts exceed expectation.
Fb2: Second. A case definition is needed before counting.
Fb3: Third. Systematic case finding follows the definition.
Fb4: Fourth. Descriptive epidemiology follows case finding.
